lessons.title: The legal framework you work in
lessons.html:
Working inside the law

During your work experience you will apply inspection procedures every day at a registered abattoir. Each procedure has a legal basis, and you must be able to show that you followed it.

Main laws

LawWhat it covers in your work
Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulationsAbattoir registration, hygiene, ante-mortem and post-mortem inspection, marking, and handling of condemned material
Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984Control and reporting of animal diseases, including notifiable diseases
Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962Humane treatment of animals during handling and slaughter
Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993Your safety and the safety of workers

How the law reaches the line

The law and regulations are broad. The abattoir turns them into written procedures: the hygiene management plan, standard operating procedures, checklists and inspection protocols for each species. The provincial veterinary services audit the abattoir and check that these procedures match the law and are followed.

Your duties as an inspector in training

  • Follow the inspection procedure for each species exactly: the right organs, the right incisions, in the right order.
  • Make judgements according to the regulations and your supervisor's or veterinarian's instructions.
  • Stay independent. Production staff may not tell you to pass a carcass.
  • Report notifiable diseases and any illegal practice, such as attempts to remove condemned meat.
  • Keep honest, complete and legible records.

Your mentor will sign off on tasks as you show you can do them. Ask questions when you are unsure. It is always better to detain and ask than to guess.

lessons.title: Applying procedures on a working day
lessons.html:
A typical inspection day

Your work experience follows the flow of a real slaughter day. At each stage, ask yourself: what does the procedure require, and have I done it?

  1. Start of shift: sign in, put on clean protective clothing, wash hands, collect knives and check sterilisers.
  2. Pre-operational check: inspect the hall and equipment against the checklist and record the result.
  3. Ante-mortem inspection: check animals and their movement documents in the lairage; separate suspects.
  4. Post-mortem inspection: head, offal and carcass at each station, using viewing, palpation and incision as required.
  5. Detention and judgement: move suspect carcasses to the detention rail with their parts; the veterinarian or senior inspector decides.
  6. Marking: apply the inspection mark only to passed carcasses; keep stamps under control.
  7. Condemned material: observe that it is marked, contained and removed correctly.
  8. Chilling and dispatch: check temperatures and loading hygiene.
  9. End of shift: complete records, hand over stamps and report any problems.

Evidence in your logbook

For work-experience modules you keep a logbook or portfolio. Record the date, the species, the number of carcasses you inspected and the conditions you found. Your mentor signs to confirm. Good entries are specific, for example: inspected 120 sheep carcasses; found 3 livers with fluke, condemned; 1 carcass with caseous lymphadenitis abscess, trimmed.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Skipping incisions when the line is busy.
  • Forgetting to sterilise the knife.
  • Losing the link between offal and carcass.
  • Filling in records at the end of the day from memory.

Key points

  • Each inspection procedure has a legal basis in the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and related laws.
  • The abattoir turns the law into written procedures that are audited by provincial veterinary services.
  • Stay independent from production pressure; when in doubt, detain and ask.
  • Record findings as they happen, not from memory.
  • Keep a specific, signed logbook of your work experience.

quiz.question: Who audits abattoirs to check that procedures match the law?

Pass it and write a note

From memory at the end of the day
